Sequential workflow
The Sequential workflow template idx_02ab5c99 provides a linear idx_d395dc3d execution pattern. Each step runs one

Choosing the right workflow type
Selecting the right idx_69081637 template depends on the level of complexity and control your solution
requires. You can use a blank workflow template for maximum flexibility, a sequential
template for straightforward linear processes, a human-in-the-loop template for governance
and oversight, and a Group chat workflow for multi-agent reasoning.
For our practical sample, we will begin with a blank workflow, then progressively incorporate
conditional logic and human review patterns. This will allow us to understand each building
block rather than relying on automation from the start.
Regardless of the template you choose, every workflow uses the same core components: nodes
connected through defined inputs and outputs.
Common node types include:
Invoke nodes for calling other agents as part of the workflow
Data transformation nodes for working with variables and dynamic values
Flow nodes that contain conditional nodes for complex decision scenarios
Basic nodes that include interactions with agents
Each node performs a specific task. This modular approach makes workflows easier to debug,
extend, and govern compared to embedding all logic inside a single prompt.

Designing structured and reliable outputs
At this point, our idx_25acf290 workflow can collect a support request and invoke an agent to analyze it.
That's a good start. But if we want this to behave like a real triage system and not just a
chatbot, we need structure and reliability.
In conversational workflows, structure is not enforced through a separate schema panel.
Instead, it's achieved through clear agent instructions and careful variable handling.
Let's refine our design.
Step 1 – Make the agent return structured JSON
Inside the Agent node, update the instructions to explicitly require JSON output. For example:
Analyze the support request and return ONLY valid JSON with the following
fields:category: billing | technical | security | generalurgency: low |
medium | highsentiment: positive | neutral | negativerisk_score: number
between 0 and 1
It's important to clearly state:
" Return ONLY valid JSON "
No additional explanations
No commentary outside the JSON object
Why? Because the next steps in the workflow depend on predictable data. If the Agent adds
extra text, downstream nodes may fail. This is one of the most important principles when
building automation with GenAI: If the output drives logic, it must be structured.
Step 2 – Extract individual fields
Now we want to idx_3445e62b operate on specific values like risk_score or urgency.

Connecting the workflow to an agent
Up to this point, we've idx_3609e4e5 been designing and testing our Support Triage Assistant directly inside
the Workflow canvas. It collects user input, invokes an agent for reasoning, parses structured
output, and routes the request based on risk.
But workflows are not meant to live in isolation. In real-world scenarios, users don't interact
with a workflow diagram; they interact with an agent experience: a chat interface, a copilot
embedded in an application, or an internal assistant exposed to employees. The workflow
defines the logic while the Agent defines the experience.
This section focuses on how to connect what we've built to something users can actually use.
111 Working with Workflows
Understanding the relationship: Workflow vs. agent
Before wiring things together, it's important to clarify roles:
Workflow: Defines execution logic and routing
Agent: Provides conversational interface and persona
In our case, the workflow performs classification, risk evaluation, and routing. The agent acts
as the user-facing assistant that initiates and drives the workflow. Think of it like this: The
workflow is the engine, and the agent is the dashboard. The engine makes decisions; the
dashboard presents them.
Step 1 – Ensure the agent is properly configured
Since our workflow idx_3086ce1a already includes an Agent node, we need to confirm that the Agent being
invoked is:
Connected to the correct model deployment
Using stable system instructions
Not adding conversational noise to structured outputs
Inside the Agent configuration (outside the workflow), verify:
The system role is clearly defined
Output instructions are explicit
No additional conversational wrapping is enforced
This matters because if the agent is configured as a "friendly conversational assistant" that
always adds commentary, your structured JSON output may break. For workflows that depend
on structured responses, precision is more important than personality.
Step 2 – Position the workflow as the entry logic
In many implementations, you will design the Workflow to handle the structured logic, while
the Agent experience becomes the front door. For example:
A user opens an internal support copilot
The copilot triggers the Support Triage Workflow
The workflow collects input, evaluates risk, and determines routing
The Agent interface displays the resulting messages
In practice, this means:
The Workflow contains the orchestration
The Agent references or invokes the workflow as part of its behavior

This separation keeps responsibilities clear. If business logic changes (for example, escalation
threshold moves from 0.7 to 0.65), you modify the workflow, not the entire conversational
experience. You idx_5966d7e0 can open the agent in the playground to ensure the configurations are correct
based on the configurations from the workflow.
Step 3 – Prepare the workflow for real use
Before exposing the workflow to real users, confirm:
All variables are properly parsed
All branches end cleanly
No execution path leaves the workflow hanging
Escalation messaging is clear and unambiguous
In particular, verify that the End nodes are placed correctly. Every possible branch must
eventually reach an End node. This ensures predictable execution and avoids unexpected
loops. Also, review user-facing messages. For example, instead of " Flagged for escalation ",
use " Your request involves a potential security risk. I'm routing this to our
support team for immediate review. " When connected to a real Agent experience, tone
becomes more visible.
Step 4 – Think about governance and boundaries
When a workflow is attached to an Agent, it becomes part of a broader AI system. That means
governance matters.
Ask yourself:
Should high-risk cases always require human review?
Should certain categories bypass automation?
Should sensitive tickets trigger logging or audit actions?
Because your workflow already parses structured data and evaluates conditions explicitly,
these policies are easy to implement. For example, add a second condition:
If ticket_category == "security" → Always escalate
That rule is now transparent, visible, and auditable — unlike hidden prompt instructions.

Deploying AI Solutions
Deploying an AI solution is the moment when your work moves from the lab into the real
world. Up to this point, you've explored data, built, and evaluated models, agent and workflow
creation with refined interactions — all within a controlled environment. Deployment is where
those agents start delivering value to users, applications, and business processes.
In Microsoft Foundry, deployment isn't just about making an agent and model accessible; it's
about ensuring it runs reliably, securely, and at the scale your use case demands. Whether
you're exposing a real-time endpoint to support instant predictions, scheduling large-scale
batch jobs, or embedding a conversational agent into an enterprise workflow, the platform
offers multiple deployment pathways to fit different needs.
As you go through this chapter, think of deployment not as a final step, but as the beginning of
a new cycle. Once your solution is live, you'll start observing how it behaves under real
conditions, how users interact with it, and where it can be improved. That feedback loop is
what ultimately turns a good AI solution into a reliable one.
In this chapter, you will learn how to deploy models, workflows, and agents using the
Microsoft Foundry portal, how to configure endpoints and access, and how to validate that
your solution is ready for real-world usage. By the end of this chapter, you will be able to take a
solution you built in Foundry and confidently deploy it so it can be consumed by applications
and users.

Understanding deployment in Microsoft Foundry
In Microsoft Foundry, deployment is idx_5f0b4692 the mechanism that allows everything you've built—
models, workflows, and agents—to be exposed as something consumable. This could be an API
endpoint, an internal assistant, or even a backend service powering an application.
At a high level, deployment idx_866eccda in Foundry is not just about "running a model." It's about
packaging intelligence into a usable interface. This is an important distinction. You are not
simply deploying infrastructure—you are deploying behavior that has been carefully designed
in previous steps.
To make this more concrete, let's break down what can actually be deployed in the Foundry
portal.
What can you deploy?
In Microsoft Foundry, you typically work with three main deployable assets:
Models: These are the idx_ff59d94d foundation. When deployed, they idx_c6e77e51 become endpoints that can
receive prompts and return responses.
Workflows: These idx_247f37de represent orchestrated logic—multiple idx_a55232e8 steps, conditions, and
transformations built on top of models. When deployed, they behave like structured
APIs.
Agents: These are idx_4ee3924a higher-level constructs that combine idx_b93b60e2 instructions, tools, and
workflows to interact with users in a more dynamic way.

If you are building something interactive, such as a customer support assistant or a copilot

Understanding edge cases in deployment selection
The decision flowchart works for typical scenarios, but real-world situations often involve
nuance. Here are the most common edge cases where the obvious choice fails:
Edge case 1: Serverless cold starts break your SLA
Scenario: You're building idx_35155c3e a customer support chatbot. Traffic is unpredictable: sometimes 10

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 130
chunks.content:
requests per hour, sometimes 100. Serverless seems perfect: you pay only for what you use, no
cluster to maintain.
The problem: Serverless endpoints have cold start latency. The first request after a period of
inactivity takes 5-15 seconds. If your customer support SLA is "response in under 2 seconds,"
serverless fails immediately.
When this matters: Any use case where sub-100ms or sub-2-second latency is critical (real-
time scoring, trading, live chat) cannot use serverless, regardless of cost savings.
The solution: Use a real-time managed endpoint with minimum replicas=1. This keeps one
instance warm, guaranteeing fast responses. Yes, you pay for idle capacity (~$50-100/month
for one replica), but your SLA is met, and users have a good experience. The cost of reliability is
worth it.
Edge case 2: You need both real-time AND batch processing
Scenario: You're building a recommendation engine. Interactive requests come from users
browsing (must respond in <2 seconds). Batch requests come nightly for analysis and model
updates (no latency requirement). The temptation is to build one solution and deploy it for
both.
The problem: Real-time and batch processing have opposite requirements. Real-time expects
sub-2-second latency, handles small payloads, and scales horizontally. Batch doesn't care
about latency, handles huge payloads, and prefers vertical scaling (more powerful compute).
When this matters: Any system with mixed interactive and bulk processing workloads.
The solution: Deploy idx_2ddeb715 twice. One real-time endpoint for interactive recommendations. One
batch job for nightly processing. They might share the same underlying model, but they're
exposed and optimized differently. This is more infrastructure to maintain, but you get the
performance you need for each workload.

Edge case 3: Compliance and data sensitivity eliminates choices
Scenario: You're processing healthcare data (PHI - Protected Health Information). Serverless
seems perfect—minimal overhead, auto-scaling, and cheap. You deploy to serverless.
The problem: Serverless infrastructure is shared with other customers. Your healthcare data is
being processed on shared infrastructure. This violates HIPAA. Your application is now non-
compliant and unusable.
When this matters: Any regulated industry (healthcare, finance, government) or any solution
processing PII.
The solution: Use AKS or Container Apps idx_83a34e01 with bring-your-own-container (BYOC). You
control the infrastructure, ensuring encryption in transit and at rest, maintaining audit logs,
and guaranteeing data never leaves your environment. This is more expensive and
operationally complex, but it's the only compliant option.
Edge case 4: Low RPS but extreme latency sensitivity
Scenario: You're building idx_413905e5 a real-time trading bot or a real-time scoring service for fraud
detection. Volume is low (maybe 5 requests per minute), but every millisecond matters. A
100ms delay costs money.
The problem: Serverless is tempting (cheap per request), but cold starts are 5-15 seconds. Even
a warm serverless instance adds 300-500 ms of platform latency.
When this matters: Low volume usually suggests serverless, but sub-100ms latency
sensitivity demands otherwise.
The solution: Use a real-time managed endpoint with minimum replicas. Accept the base cost
of maintaining warm capacity. The latency requirement overrides cost optimization.
Edge case 5: Migration from prototype to production
Scenario: You start with a prototype on serverless. It's cheap and quick. But as users adopt it
and traffic grows to 100+ RPS, you hit cold start issues during business hours.
The problem: Requests that were fine at 10 RPS are now unacceptable at 100 RPS.
When this matters: Your deployment strategy should evolve as your solution matures.
The solution: Set up monitoring on cold start latency. When it exceeds your SLA, migrate to
real-time managed inference. This is a natural progression: prototype cheap and fast, migrate
to reliable and scalable as demand grows.

Common deployment scenarios and troubleshooting
Things happen, and you should idx_0fd41155 have a plan to remediate them. Here are some scenarios that
can happen and what to check.
Scenario 1: Deployment seems stuck
In this scenario, check whether the page needs to be refreshed, as the UI may not
always update in real time. Then, review the logs in the Operate section to see whether
any errors are reported. If the issue is still not resolved after 10 minutes, try redeploying
the asset, as a permission issue is often the cause.
Scenario 2: Deployment completes, but endpoint returns errors
If the deployment completes successfully but the endpoint returns errors, start by
testing the endpoint directly from the Playground. This helps you determine whether
the issue is with the endpoint itself or with the application calling it. Next, check the
Traces tab in the Operate section to see which requests are reaching the endpoint. You
should also verify that the input schema matches what the calling systems are sending,
especially if the deployed asset is a workflow.
Scenario 3: Cost is higher than expected
If the deployment costs more than expected, begin by checking token usage in Operate
> Metrics to see whether traffic is higher than planned. For provisioned deployments,
review whether the asset is hitting rate limits, as this can sometimes trigger expensive
fallback behavior. If multiple asset versions are deployed at the same time, consider
consolidating to one active version to reduce unnecessary cost.
Scenario 4: Want to update the deployed asset
When updating a deployed asset, the best practice is to deploy the new version
alongside the old version, using a clear name such as gpt ‑ v2 next to gpt ‑ v1. Test the
new version thoroughly before retiring the old one. This approach, often called blue-
green idx_8eaf3da5 deployment, gives you a rollback path if the new version has issues.
Make this list as large as the cases you have detected during deployment. Document the triage
process and the next steps for each of them.
Troubleshooting helps you respond when something goes wrong, but a stronger deployment
process also reduces the impact of problems before they happen. One of the best ways to do
that is to avoid changing live assets directly. Instead, each meaningful change should be
released as a separate version that can be tested, compared, and rolled back if needed. This is
where a clear versioning strategy becomes important.

Once an asset is deployed, it becomes idx_c48b646f part of a live system. Any change to that asset can affect
calling applications, connected workflows, or users who depend on the current behavior. For
that reason, you should avoid modifying production assets directly. A safer approach is to

how to monitor real production traffic, analyze performance and token usage, set up logging
and governance controls, and introduce human oversight when risk levels demand it. In other

If you've worked in technology long enough (and I know many of you have), you've probably

An AI application can appear to work perfectly during development. Prompts look good.

language, real edge cases, and real pressure — things change. Subtle hallucinations appear.
Tone shifts. Costs spike. Safety filters behave inconsistently. And the problem is not that the
model is "bad"; the problem is that we didn't evaluate and monitor it properly.
That's where this chapter begins. Let's go into more detail about this journey when we talk
about evaluating and monitoring AI applications and agents.

as part of the lifecycle. It lives inside your project, next to your deployments, datasets, and

separate from AI development — it is part of it.

Also, in this journey, AI idx_66e78179 systems rarely fail loudly. A chatbot may answer 95% of questions
correctly, but subtly mislead users on the remaining 5%. A summarization model may omit a
critical sentence. A content generation workflow may pass safety filters in staging but behave
differently with real-world phrasing.
And here's the uncomfortable truth: if you're not measuring these behaviors, you won't see
them. For example:
A customer support assistant performs well in internal testing, but in production, it
may start giving overly confident answers instead of escalating complex issues
A sales copilot generates persuasive emails, but occasionally it may invent product
features that don't exist
A healthcare triage assistant responds most of the time accurately, but it may
misinterpret ambiguous symptoms in rare edge cases
None of these issues is visible through manual testing alone. They require structured
evaluation and ongoing monitoring.
To make this concrete, consider idx_22f999e0 a well-documented case that became a reference point in AI
liability discussions. A major airline deployed a customer-facing chatbot to handle common

queries, including questions about bereavement travel policies. A passenger asked the chatbot
whether a discounted bereavement fare could be claimed after the trip. The chatbot said yes —
and even provided instructions for submitting the request within 90 days. The passenger
booked a full-price ticket based on that guidance and submitted the reimbursement request
afterward. The airline denied it. The actual policy did not allow retroactive claims.
The company argued it could not be held responsible for the chatbot's misleading information,
going as far as claiming the chatbot should be considered a separate entity — and therefore
absolved of any liability for its inaccuracies. The tribunal rejected that argument entirely,
finding that the airline owed the passenger a duty of care and had failed to exercise reasonable
care to ensure the chatbot's information was accurate and not misleading.
The technical failure was not dramatic. The model did not produce offensive content or go
wildly off-script. It generated a nonexistent policy — confidently, coherently, and in a context
where the user had every reason to trust it. That is precisely the kind of failure that manual
testing misses: it behaves correctly in most cases, sounds authoritative, and only breaks under
specific conditions unlikely to appear in a curated test dataset. Springer
What a proper evaluation and monitoring pipeline would have caught:
Groundedness evaluation would have flagged that the chatbot's response was not
grounded in the actual policy documentation — a discrepancy that shows up clearly

Scheduled human review sampling on high-stakes response categories would have

The tribunal idx_33716f95 award represented only the visible tip of the cost iceberg. The full business impact
extended well beyond the damages paid—legal representation, policy review, public scrutiny,
and reputational damage that no tribunal fee covers.
This is not a story about a model being bad. It is a story about an organization that deployed a
customer-facing AI system without the evaluation and monitoring infrastructure to catch
what it was getting wrong. The tools existed. The discipline did not.

Types of evaluation
Foundry evaluation isn't only about "is the answer correct?" That would be too narrow for
modern GenAI apps. In practice, most teams need a blend of quality, safety, and reliability
checks.
Here are the most common evaluation styles you'll run into inside a Project:
Model/Deployment evaluation: Evaluate idx_a609e43d a deployed model idx_3c24cbc0 endpoint using a dataset
of prompts (and optionally expected answers). This is the most straightforward and is
usually where teams start.
Prompt or response quality evaluation: Useful when the "model is fine" but the
output varies because idx_cf74bc53 your prompt or system instructions changed. This idx_e15a3760 is common
when you're iterating on tone, formatting, or tool-use behavior.
Workflow evaluation: If your idx_da81c743 app is not a single call to a model — for idx_015289b2 example, it uses
retrieval, tool calls, branching logic, or multi-step reasoning — you want to evaluate
the entire flow, not just the final answer.
Safety evaluation: This is idx_97b01858 where you measure policy alignment: unsafe idx_32b312cb content,
jailbreak behavior, refusal patterns, and how well your guardrails hold up under
adversarial prompts.
A practical way to think about it is:
Quality: Is it helpful and correct?
Safety: Is it appropriate and compliant?
Reliability: Is it consistent across real-world variation?
